exit_trigger: Evidence that customers can switch additive suppliers without qualification friction or price concessions; Structural decline in demand for the company's core products from long-term shifts in the end markets; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5; Management capital allocation that destroys value, such as buybacks at inflated prices or poor acquisitions; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value
rationale: The numbers I was handed look attractive: a 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, a market cap of about $6.7 billion, and a price of $714.94 against a model value of $1,271.73. But I won't buy on a model alone. That value rests on 8% growth for ten years at a 5% discount rate, and the snapshot gives me no 10-year earnings record, no CEO tenure, no ROIC and no description of the business. Debt-to-equity of 0.497 clears my 0.5 ceiling by a whisker. Owner earnings are only about 6.1% of market cap, which is thin against the 10-year Treasury plus 4% yield check. The snapshot does not report the Treasury yield, so I cannot confirm that check passes. Until I can verify those pieces and see whether the additive franchise holds up over the next decade, I'm sitting on my hands. I'm not rejecting it, but I'm not paying either.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing-power erosion, such as sustained discounting or margin compression; Loss of market share to competitors in premium athletic apparel; Management capital-allocation failures or dishonest reporting; Price exceeding 1.5x a verified intrinsic value with a persistent gap
rationale: Lululemon is a premium athletic apparel brand that I can describe in two paragraphs, so it sits inside my circle. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 34.6% and a debt-to-equity of 0.0, and a market cap of about $12.2 billion. The model's intrinsic value of $346.97 against a $110.69 price implies a 68% margin of safety. That is too good to take at face value. It rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not trust it until I know why the market is so pessimistic. The snapshot says nothing on earnings consistency, same-store trends, competition, or management, and fashion-driven apparel is exactly where a moat has to be rebuilt every season. Until I can check those things, I am watching, not buying. Rule No. 1 is not to lose money.

exit_trigger: If bought later: evidence that service and parts earnings are eroding; Sustained decline in margins or ROE below 15% with no clear cause; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5; Management capital allocation errors, such as buybacks at prices well above intrinsic value or poor acquisitions; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value, with the gap persisting
rationale: I understand the basic business: a dealership group that sells cars and services them. The numbers I was handed look good: a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39, and a price about 18% below a no-growth owner-earnings value of $259.62 a share. But I have not been shown a durable moat, and a retailer of other people's products usually competes on thin differentiation. This snapshot also contains no 10-year earnings history, no margin data, and nothing on management or capital allocation. A cheap-looking price on a business whose moat I cannot prove is how I bought Dexter Shoe. I will keep this on the watch list and wait for evidence of consistent earnings and pricing power before I commit capital.

exit_trigger: Evidence that brands can no longer hold price without losing volume (moat erosion); Management making large acquisitions that destroy value or showing opaque reporting; Leverage materially above 0.5 debt-to-equity; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: Packaged food is a business I can explain: a portfolio of familiar pantry and snack brands sold through grocers. On the numbers I was given, this looks cheap. The price is $23.28 against a $43.71 estimate, a 46.7% margin of safety, with a 5-year ROE of 21.7% and debt-to-equity of 0.10. But that estimate assumes zero growth, and the snapshot is silent on the things I insist on: ten years of earnings, how management has allocated capital, and any evidence the brands can still raise prices. Debt-to-equity looks low enough that I want to confirm the debt is fully captured, because untagged debt is not the same as no debt. A cheap price on an unverified record is how I ended up with a textile mill, so I will wait for the evidence before paying anything.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or gross margins versus online and large-scale distributors; Loss of key supplier or customer relationships that weakens the scale advantage; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with a persistent gap

I will put this on the watch list and wait until I can verify what is missing.

exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion, such as loss of pricing power or private-label and low-cost competitors taking share; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Dishonest or opaque reporting from management; Price persistently above 1.5x intrinsic value
rationale: Paints, sealants and protective coatings are a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the numbers in front of me look good: a 5-year average ROE of about 22.9% and a margin of safety of about 19% against a DCF value of $133.59 per share. The reported debt-to-equity of 0.0027 looks too low for a company like this, so I suspect the debt is untagged rather than absent, and a company whose debt is untagged is not a company without debt. I also have no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure or capital allocation history, and no ROIC in this snapshot. So I'll sit on my hands, keep the name on the list, and revisit once those gaps are filled.
